title: James Webb spots a strange change in Chariklo's invisible rings
excerpt: A cosmic surprise from the Webb.
content:
For centuries it was believed that rings could only be found on the giant planets, on Saturn with its brilliant rings, on Jupiter with its thin halo, on Uranus with its dark arcs, and on Neptune with its icy fragments.

However, in 2013 astronomers came across something remarkable: Chariklo, a small object with a diameter of just 250 kilometers that orbits between Saturn and Uranus, has two dense rings. It was the first minor body found to possess such a system.

Now, new observations with the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) have revealed that Chariklo’s rings are not static ornaments frozen in time. They are changing, on timescales of just a few years.

On October 18, 2022, the Institute of Astrophysics of Andalusia (IAA-CSIC) led a daring experiment. Using JWST, they observed Chariklo as it passed in front of a distant star, a stellar occultation.

By measuring the star’s light as Chariklo and its rings blocked it, astronomers could study the rings indirectly, since they are far too narrow and distant to photograph directly.

The results, published in Science Advances, were startling. Comparing JWST’s data with earlier occultations, researchers found that Chariklo’s inner ring had grown more opaque, while the outer ring had become more transparent. In other words, the two rings were evolving in opposite directions.

Up to now, scientists had thought that rings orbiting small bodies were fairly stable. However, Chariklo’s changing opacity casts doubt on that idea and implies that ring systems around minor bodies could be dynamic, evolving structures formed through complex processes which we do not yet fully understand.

As lead researcher Pablo Santos-Sanz explained: “Our results force us to rethink how they form, how they evolve, and what mechanisms maintain their stability.”

It is not known what the physical cause of these changes is; they might be due to true temporal evolution, to differences in the observational filters, or to a combination of these two factors.

The study was also a milestone in space observation. This was the first stellar occultation ever predicted and observed with JWST. Achieving it required extraordinary precision: knowing Chariklo’s orbit, the star’s position (thanks to ESA’s Gaia mission), and JWST’s trajectory around the L2 Lagrange point, 1.5 million kilometers from Earth.

At the moment of occultation, Chariklo’s relative speed to JWST was just 2.5 km/s, providing unprecedented resolution. This allowed astronomers to probe the rings’ fine structure in detail.

Chariklo’s evolving rings open a new frontier. If such small systems can change measurably within a decade, then ring dynamics may be far more complex than previously thought. The discovery could reshape our understanding of how rings form, persist, and dissipate, not only around Chariklo, but around other small bodies and even giant planets.

It also shows off the capability of the JWST to study phenomena that cannot be seen through direct imaging; astronomers are discovering secrets of worlds that are too small and faint to be seen directly by observing the shadows that flicker across distant stars.

Journal Reference:

  1. Pablo Santos-Sanz, Altair R. Gomes-Junior, Bruno Morgado et al. JWST stellar occultation reveals unexpected changes in Chariklo’s ring system. Science Advances. DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aeh4794
